scope: One additional living headshield slug for the existing species guide, optional identification activity and illustrative reef encounters. New copy is paraphrased from museum accounts and research. Field marks support learning from the model, not guaranteed field identification.
iucnYearConvention: No reliable current global IUCN assessment was located. SeaLifeBase’s IUCN2025-2 export reports Not Evaluated, so use NE with a null assessment year. This is not a statement that the species is secure.

specimens.name: Blue velvet headshield slug
marks: Deep black body outlined by thin, vivid blue lines
A broad headshield with a blue line along its centre
Raised side flaps, called parapodia, partly wrap around the body
Two tapering, tail-like lobes extend behind the body and are unequal in length
specimens.role: Small predator that specializes in free-living flatworms around reef-associated sediment.
specimens.fact: Although sometimes called a blue velvet nudibranch, it is a headshield slug in a different sea-slug group.
specimens.habitat: Sand around reefs and sandy reef slopes across the tropical Indo-West Pacific.
specimens.diet: Small flatworms, including acoels documented in feeding records. It is a specialist predator, rather than an algae grazer.
specimens.behavior: Crawls across the bottom. Individuals may follow another slug’s mucus trail, sometimes before mating.
specimens.observe: Trace the blue outlines, folded side flaps and unequal tail lobes. Compare these with the exposed gill plume and rhinophores on Anna’s chromodoris.

specimens.caution: NE does not mean secure. The 3cm maximum in SeaLifeBase is explicitly assumed from a field guide and is not used over the museum’s approximately7cm account and larger documented photographs. Tail length and colour lines may vary or be altered by damage. The left posterior lobe is modeled longer, consistent with the usual morphology, but the learner-facing mark says unequal rather than always left-longer. The closest similarly coloured headshield species are not already in this guide; the nudibranch comparison is a teaching contrast, not a claim of taxonomic closeness or reliable identification from a simplified model. No aquarium pest-eradication, toxicity, obligatory nocturnality or complete wild prey-list claim is made.

modelProvenance.basis: An illustrative5cm adult, consistent with museum-reviewed photographs. About7cm is the museum species-account maximum. The5–30m metadata interval brackets documented museum-reviewed encounters; it is not a physiological or exhaustive distributional boundary.
modelProvenance.anatomy: Broad headshield with small anterior lobes, dark smooth body, thin blue marginal lines and median head line, raised folded parapodia, and two tapering posterior mantle lobes. The left lobe can be longer in this illustrative individual. No exposed dorid-style dorsal gill plume or paired rhinophores.
modelProvenance.anatomyLimits: Museum sources explicitly support unequal lobes. Left-longer is consistent with published genus morphology and species photographs, but not treated as an invariant identification rule. Fine internal anatomy and full wild colour variation are not represented.
modelProvenance.motion: Low-amplitude side-flap and tail-lobe flex while the foot remains grounded. Crawling and current movement are artistic teaching choices, not measured gait data; avoid continuous free swimming or a pulsing jellyfish shape.

integration.lookalikeNote: The existing nudibranch is Chromodoris annae. Its blue-black body may prompt a useful novice comparison, while its orange border, exposed gill plume and rhinophores differ. Keep the new link one-way; do not modify the existing nudibranch record.
integration.identificationLimit: The illustrated field marks support learning and comparison. They are not a promise of definitive real-world species identification.
